list.listitem: Glaucoma is diagnosed in most patients by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), optic neuropathy, and glaucomatous visual field loss. C
Patients should be referred to ophthalmology if glaucoma is suspected. C
The only effective treatment for glaucoma with elevated IOP is to decrease and control IOP with medications and/or surgery to prevent progression of structural or functional loss. A
Acute angle closure glaucoma is an ocular emergency that requires immediate lowering of IOP with topical/oral/parenteral medications or laser peripheral iridotomy. A

Glaucoma is defined as damage to the optic nerve (optic neuropathy) and retinal nerve fiber layer leading to visual field defects. Untreated, this progressive disease causes permanent optic nerve damage and subsequent visual field loss that can result in blindness. There are approximately 60 types of glaucoma. The most common type, accounting for approximately 90% of cases, is primary open angle glaucoma (POAG). The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO, 2020) defines POAG as a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy in adults in which there is a characteristic acquired atrophy of the optic nerve and loss of retinal ganglion cells and their axons. The condition is associated with an open anterior chamber angle by gonioscopy. POAG is often bilateral, subacute in onset, and associated with elevated IOP, and more common in adults over age 40. Acute primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is an ophthalmologic emergency. It typically has an acute onset of optic neuropathy and visual loss similar to POAG with a closed anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy.
In a population study of 1986 subjects over age 49 years in Australia, 3.4% developed POAG by 10-year follow-up.

Among individuals with ocular hypertension enrolled in the European Glaucoma Prevention Study who also participated in the Heidelberg Retina Tomograph ancillary study, 61/489 (12.5%) developed OAG at 5 years. Baseline parameters associated with OAG development included "outside normal limits" classification of the Frederick Mikelberg discriminant, larger mean cup depth and/or volume, cup-to-disc area ratio, cup area, smaller rim area, and cup shape measure. Hazard ratios ranged from 1.18 to 2.51.
As of 2022, approximately 4.22 million people in the US have glaucoma.

The overall prevalence of POAG in the US population 40 years and older was estimated at 1.86% (95% CI, 1.75%-1.96%) in 2004. Prevalence of POAG is higher among those of Latino/Hispanic (4.74%, 95% CI 4.22-5.30) and African ancestry (3.4%).

A similar figure of 2.1% (95% CI, 1.7%-2.6%) was found for POAG based on optic nerve fundus photography in the non-institutionalized US civilian population aged 40 years and older participating in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2005-2008.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 papers including 26,993 patients in Europe found a slightly higher pooled prevalence of POAG of 2.60% (95% CI 1.90%-3.56%).

In a community-based cross sectional observational study of 8623 participants in Norwich UK, 4% had glaucoma present in either eye and 10% had ocular hypertension. Of those with glaucoma, 87% had POAG.
In a population-based study in Finland of 10,321 patients aged 45-49 years of whom half were randomized to eye screening, definite glaucoma was found in 33 subjects (1.1%; 95% CI, 0.8-1.5).
Pooled prevalence of PACG among adult Asian patients was found to be 0.75% (95% CI, 0.58-0.96).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 55 population-based studies worldwide, including 189,359 participants of whom 6949 were found to have some form of glaucoma, reported that more than half of glaucoma cases were previously undetected in each geographical region. Higher odds of having undetected glaucoma occurred in Africa and Asia compared with Europe.
Total direct costs for patients diagnosed with glaucoma for ages 40 to 64 years were US$1.8 billion and for those 65 years or older were US$1.1 billion.
Glaucoma contributes to the overall indirect costs of blindness (US$11 billion dollars) and to the overall loss of productivity due to blindness (US$8.0 billion).
Glaucoma is the second leading cause of global blindness.
There are an estimated 5.2 million people blind from glaucoma which accounts for 15% of the total world blindness. PACG accounts for 50% of glaucoma blindness worldwide.
Quality of life decreases with increased glaucoma severity.
Glaucoma is a risk factor for retinal vein occlusion with an OR of 4.01; 95% CI, 3.28-4.91, based on a meta-analysis of 15 observational studies.
Siblings of individuals with POAG have a ten-fold increased risk of developing POAG.

Authors of one study used a meta-analysis to obtain heritability (h2) estimates for glaucoma and its related endophenotypes (10 clusters including IOP, anterior chamber and cup-to-disc ratio). The h2 for POAG ranged from 0.17 to 0.81; the h2 for PACG was 0.65, based on a single study; and pooled h2 for IOP was 0.43 (95% CI, 0.38-0.48.
Unknown. See below for risk factors.

A number of genetic susceptibility alleles are associated with POAG in White identifying people; these appear to have a greatly reduced role in populations of African ancestry. There is a significant association of Glutathione S-transferase M1 null genotype with POAG risk in East Asians.
In the Australian study cited above, two loci associated with cup-to-disc ratio (9p21 near CDKN2B-AS1 and SIX1/SIX6) were both significantly associated with incident OAG.

Authors of a genome-wide meta-analysis identified 9 new genomic regions associated with vertical cup-disc ratio, one new region associated with IOP, 5 novel loci for optic nerve cup area and 6 novel loci for disc area.
Glaucoma can also result from post penetrating keratoplasty; pooled incidence in one meta-analysis of IOP >21 mmHg was 21.5%; 95% CI, 17.8 to 25.7.

All types of glaucoma have an associated IOP that is elevated for that individual. This may be due to a variety of anomalies such as significant trabecular meshwork (TM) resistance to outflow of aqueous humor, lack of aqueous humor access to the TM, clogging of the TM with inflammatory cells, neovascularization, or tumor cells, and dysgenesis of the TM or other anterior segment structures.

Two mechanisms are proposed for how elevated IOP causes visual field loss. The first theory is that mechanical compression of the anterior optic nerve axons disrupts the axoplasmic flow with subsequent neuronal atrophy. The second theory is that optic nerve ischemia is caused by decreased optic nerve perfusion. This may be related to abnormal vascular autoregulation.

Glaucoma prevalence increases with increasing intraocular pressure (IOP). In the Baltimore Eye Survey, published in 1991, nearly 7% of White identifying people and 25% of African American/Black identifying people had POAG at an IOP of 30 mmHg. However, over half of all glaucomatous eyes had a screening IOP below 21 mm Hg regardless of treatment status
IOP elevation is associated with sleep positions, with the lateral decubitus position most favorable, but its influence on glaucoma progression is uncertain.
Oxidative stress may also play a key role in several types of eye disease including glaucoma.

Use of intravitreous injections of ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema
Uveitis treated with fluocinolone acetonide implant

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (2022) does not recommend for or against screening adults for glaucoma in persons 40 years or older with no symptoms of glaucoma (I recommendation). There is insufficient evidence to determine the extent to which the earlier detection and treatment of people with elevated IOP or POAG reduces impairment in vision-related function or quality of life.

The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO, 2020) suggests that targeted screening of high-risk individuals such as older adults, those with a family history of glaucoma, and African race or Latino/Hispanic ethnicity may be more cost-effective. Although there are three methods that have been used for screening – IOP, assessment of the optic nerve head and retinal nerve fiber layer, and visual field testing – none provide high diagnostic precision for identifying cases of glaucoma. C

The potential benefit of screening is that there is good evidence that it reduces the number of persons who develop small, visual field defects and that early treatment of those with early, asymptomatic POAG decreases the number of those whose visual field defects progress.

However, this must be balanced against good evidence that treatment of increased IOP and early POAG results in a number of harms, including local eye irritation and an increased risk for cataracts. In addition, most individuals with elevated IOP at screening do not have, and may never develop, optic nerve damage.

In one screening trial of individuals attending a free health clinic, 1380 of 3004 (46%) screened positive based on history or distance visual acuity. While 81% of those who screened positive were referred for an eye exam, less than half followed through. Of those attending, one third had 1 or more problems requiring intervention including refraction, glaucoma or suspected glaucoma (8.9%), visually significant cataract (7.2%), and diabetic retinopathy (2.5%).

Combined spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (produces high-resolution images of the retina) with standard automated perimetry to assess visual fields has a sensitivity for glaucomatous damage of 44%, specificity of 97.5%, and positive predictive value of 12%, with an estimated area under the curve of 0.76.

Telemedicine presents an opportunity for remote screening. In one study of 906 African-American, Hispanic/Latino, or Asian individuals, obtaining two posterior fundus photographs and one anterior segment photograph resulted in high rates of abnormalities being identified by a trained retina reader and a glaucoma specialist including suspicious optic nerves (28.5%), ocular hypertension (11.3%), and retinal pathology (7.5%).
Frequency-doubling technology perimetry lacks both sensitivity and specificity for glaucoma screening.

In a Chinese RCT of 889 patients with suspected PACG in which one eye was treated and the other observed, the eye randomized to laser peripheral iridotomy prophylaxis had a lower incidence of primary angle closure disease (defined as a composite endpoint of elevated IOP, peripheral anterior synechiae, or acute angle-closure) during 72 months of follow-up than the non-treated eye (4.19 per 1000 eye-years vs. 7.97 per 1000 eye-years, respectively). There were few cases of incident PACG overall - 19 cases among treated eyes and 36 cases among untreated eyes.

The AAO 2020 guideline recommends diagnosing glaucoma using clinical examination of the optic nerve head; imaging of the optic nerve head, retinal nerve fiber layer and macula; and assessment of the visual field. C The evaluation may require more than one visit.
IOP measurement is usually >21 mm Hg in patients with glaucoma (except in normal tension glaucoma). C

Optic disc examination and photography/imaging show enlarged cup-to-disc ratio, cup/disc asymmetry of >0.2 in both eyes, disc hemorrhages, and/or focal loss of neuroretinal rim—all with progression over time.
Visual field perimetry shows repeatable glaucomatous field defects, not respecting vertical midline, that progress over time. C
Measurement of limbal anterior chamber depth (LACD) appeared useful for case-detection of occludable angles in patients at high-risk for PACG. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Normal optic nerve and visual field
Normal IOP and no progression of cup/disc ratio over time
Normal IOP, optic nerve pallor >cupping, visual field defects larger than expected
Calcific lesions on ultrasound/CT, stable or progressive field loss unrelated to IOP

list.listitem: The AAO 2020 guideline uses the following characteristics to define POAG severity:
Mild: characteristic optic disc, retinal nerve fiber layer, or macular imaging abnormalities consistent with glaucoma and a normal visual field as tested with standard automated perimetry.
Moderate: characteristic optic nerve abnormalities as above consistent with glaucoma and visual field abnormalities in 1 hemifield and not within 5 degrees of fixation.

Severe: characteristic optic nerve abnormalities as above consistent with glaucoma and visual field abnormalities in both hemifields and/or loss within 5 degrees of fixation in at least 1 hemifield as tested with standard automated perimetry.
Classification of PACG includes the following:
Primary angle-closure suspect (>180 degrees iridotrabecular contact (ITC), normal IOP, and no optic nerve damage)
Primary angle closure (>180 degrees ITC with peripheral anterior synechiae [PAS] or elevated IOP, but no optic neuropathy)
Primary angle-closure glaucoma (>180 degrees ITC with PAS, elevated IOP, and optic neuropathy)
Acute angle-closure crisis (occluded angle with symptomatic high IOP)

Plateau iris configuration (any ITC persisting after a patent laser peripheral iridotomy) or syndrome (any ITC persisting after a patent laser peripheral iridotomy with pressure elevation after dilation)

Patients with POAG and chronic angle-closure glaucoma are usually asymptomatic until decreased visual acuity occurs as a result of advanced disease. Patients with acute angle-closure glaucoma usually complain of red painful eye; blurred vision with haloes; and headache, nausea, and vomiting.

Obtain a personal medical history, family history of glaucoma, history of drugs which may induce angle closure including steroid use, and history of prior episodes. Risk factors for POAG include high myopia (>6 diopters), a first-degree relative with glaucoma, African heritage, Latino/Hispanic ethnicity, advanced age, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Examine pupils, which may show a relative afferent pupillary defect with asymmetrical involvement, or may be mid-dilated in acute PACG. Check visual acuity, which tends to be decreased with acute PACG.
When suspecting a visual field defect, description of a face and finger counting alone or combined has the highest positive likelihood ratios (35, 25, 43 respectively) for ruling in a visual defect.

Check IOP, which is generally >21 mm Hg with POAG and significantly higher with acute PACG (as high as 50-60 mm Hg). Preferred method is contact applanation (applying a flat-tipped cone to temporarily flatten the cornea); record time of day because of diurnal variation. Although increased IOP increases the risk of glaucoma, no single or combined physical finding(s) effectively rule out glaucoma.

Perform slit lamp exam of cornea, conjunctiva, and anterior chamber. Perform gonioscopic exam to measure anterior chamber angle to rule out angle closure or secondary causes. The AAO recommends dark room gonioscopy for diagnosis of PACG to evaluate angle anatomy, presence of iridotrabecular contact and/or peripheral anterior synechiae, and plateau iris configuration. POAG is associated with an open anterior chamber angle by gonioscopy.

Perform optic nerve exam for enlarged cup/disc ratio, cup-to-disc (CDR) asymmetry of >0.2 in both eyes, disc hemorrhages, or focal loss of neuroretinal rim. Increased optic CDR and/or increased cup-to-disc asymmetry between a patient's eyes increase the risk of glaucoma.

AAO (2020) stresses that measuring central corneal thickness (thin is a risk factor), optic nerve head, retinal nerve fiber layer and macula (based on stereoscopic disc photographs and computerized images showing structural abnormalities), and visual fields (for defects) are particularly important for diagnosis.
Assess visual field using standard automated perimetry with Swedish Interactive Threshold Algorithm, which has 98% sensitivity and 96% specificity for detecting glaucomatous visual field defect.
The AAO (2020) suggests adjusting computerized visual field programs (24 degrees, 30 degrees, 10 degrees) and stimulus size (III, V) to aid in detecting and monitoring progressive visual field loss.
A free iPad app for performing visual field testing had moderate correlation coefficients for detecting moderate and advanced visual field loss.
Photographs of the optic nerves are recommended to document progression of disease.
The AAO recommends computer-based imaging and magnified stereoscopic photography as important adjuncts to a good clinical exam.

Authors of a meta-analysis found that algorithms based on deep learning of digital fundus images had high sensitivity and specificity (0.90; 95% CI, 0.90-0.91 and 0.94; 95% CI, 0.93-0.94, respectively) for automatic diagnosis of glaucomatous optic neuropathy with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.98. These systems could be used for population screening.

If available, evaluate optic nerve head and retinal nerve fiber layer imaging with optical coherence tomography (OCT), confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy, or scanning laser polarimetry. In one study, using spectral-domain OCT, the Random Forests method performed best for diagnosing early-stage glaucoma (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.93).

The accuracy of anterior-segment-OCT against gonioscopy for diagnosing angle closure was evaluated in a meta-analysis of 23 studies; authors found a sensitivity ranging from 46 to 100% (median 87%) and specificity ranging from 55.3 to 100% (median 84%). They concluded that the test can’t replace gonioscopy.
OCT angiography can identify the significant reduction in mean peripapillary vessel density that is associated with glaucoma.
In one study comparing imaging devices in glaucoma detection, diagnostic accuracy odds ratios were 29.5 for OCT, 18.6 for scanning laser polarimetry, and 13.9 for Heidelberg Retinal Tomography (HRT).

In another study of 943 adult patients with suspected glaucoma or ocular hypertension, of four automated imaging test algorithms, HRT had the highest sensitivity (87%) but lowest specificity (63.9%), while scanning laser polarimetry (SLP) had the lowest sensitivity (35.1%) but highest specificity (97.2%) for diagnosing glaucoma. All tests missed some patients with severe glaucoma (5%-21% of eyes). Further research on diagnostic accuracy of these tests is needed.

Authors of a Cochrane review of non-contact tests for identification of PACG found limbal anterior chamber depth had potential for case-detection of occludable angles in high-risk populations. LACD ≤25% had a sensitivity 0.83 (95% CI, 0.74-0.90) and specificity of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.84-0.92) with moderate-certainty based on 16 studies with 7540 eyes. Based on their analysis, performing LACD on 1000 people at risk of angle closure with a prevalence of occludable angles of 10%, LACD would miss about 17 cases out of the 100 with occludable angles and incorrectly classify 108 out of 900 without angle closure.

Color Doppler imaging of retrobulbar vessel blood flow of the eyes appears to be useful as a diagnostic tool for POAG because glaucoma is closely related to ocular blood flow changes. Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies found that optic nerve head mean blur rate, a measure of blood flow rate measured using laser speckle flowgraphy, was significantly reduced in glaucomatous eyes.

Patients with PACG typically present with red, painful eye, blurred vision, headache, nausea, and/or vomiting. PACG is an ocular emergency, and patients should be immediately referred to an ophthalmologist.

Most patients with other forms of glaucoma are asymptomatic; they may report visual field loss. Routine referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of visual fields, slit lamp examination, and other studies is recommended, especially for patients with risk factors.
The AAO (2020) suggests an initial treatment goal of reducing IOP by 20% to 30% below baseline and to adjust up or down as indicated by disease course and severity.
Decreasing IOP is the only clinically-proven effective treatment for glaucoma; this can be achieved with medical treatment, laser surgery, filtering surgery, or cyclodestructive surgery. A
Target IOP is an individualized goal that is expected to prevent progression of structural and/or functional loss. C

For newly-diagnosed patients with POAG, interim results from a single RCT found that intensive therapy using drugs from three different classes plus 360° laser trabeculoplasty resulted in a lower median perimetric rate of progression compared to monotherapy at 3 years. B
For early POAG, medical therapy is as effective as filtering surgery without the possible sequelae of surgery. A
For PACG, topical and systemic aqueous suppressants are usually necessary to adequately decrease the IOP and laser iridotomy or iridectomy is the definitive surgical treatment. A

For patients with POAG, prostaglandin analogues (PGAs) and beta antagonists are the usual first choice. Alpha-2-blockers, topical and oral sympathomimetics, and parasympathomimetics are alternatives. PGAs act by increasing outflow of aqueous humor primarily through the uveoscleral pathway and beta-blockers act by decreasing production of aqueous humor through blockade of sympathetic nerve endings in the ciliary epithelium.

Based on interim 3-year results from the ongoing Glaucoma Intensive Treatment Study of 242 treatment-naïve, newly-diagnosed patients with POAG, those randomized to intensive therapy using drugs from three different classes plus 360° laser trabeculoplasty had a lower median perimetric rate of progression of -0.1%/year compared to -0.5%/year in the monotherapy group. The median IOP lower in the multi-treatment arm (~14 mmHg vs. ~17 mmHg) and pressures remained stable in both groups. Treatment was intensified in 42% of the mono-treated patients and 7% of the multi-treated patients.

Increased adherence with glaucoma medication was found with tailored care, which included face-to-face needs assessment and a personalized care plan, compared to standard care (SMD 1.28; 95% CI 0.08-2.48) based on a meta-analysis of 19 RCTs with 4981 participants. Additional increases in adherence were achieved with interventions adding multimedia education and device reminders (see behavioral medicine below).
In an RCT of 516 patients with newly diagnosed POAG, latanoprost 0·005% eye drops, a PGA, were more effective than placebo drops in lowering IOP and preserving visual fields.

Authors of a meta-analysis of drugs and drug combinations for lowering IOP concluded that PGAs provided the best IOP lowering effect among all monotherapy regimens and combination PGA and other category of drugs lead to better IOP decrease than dual therapy with two non-PGA drugs. PGA alone resulted in more severe hyperemia than any other monotherapy regimen, while beta antagonists had the lowest incidence of hyperemia.

Comparing three PGAs - 0.005% latanoprost, 0.004% travoprost, and 0.03% bimatoprost - in patients with POAG or ocular hypertension, authors of a meta-analysis found similar IOP reduction between latanoprost and travoprost but bimatoprost was most effective after 3-6 months of treatment; however, latanoprost was better tolerated.

In an RCT of 83 patients who were latanoprost non-responders after one month of treatment, the mean reduction in IOP was not significantly different between patients randomized to continued latanoprost, travoprost, or bimatoprost (-0.9 mmHg, -2.5 mmHg and -2.1 mmHg, respectively). About one third of all patients became responders with no significant difference between groups (31% on latanoprost, 43.5% on travoprost, and 41.9% on bimatoprost.

For patients requiring multiple medications, fixed combination medication preparations may improve adherence over combined separate preparations. A fixed combined preparation also further lowered IOP when single agents failed to achieve adequate control.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 trials found similar IOP-lowering effects for fixed-dose latanoprost/timolol, travoprost/timolol and dorzolamide/timolol based on moderate-quality evidence. Compared to latanoprost/timolol, bimatoprost/timolol resulted in a lower mean IOP.

Initial testing of a biodegradable sustained-release PGA (bimatoprost) implant demonstrated safety and effectiveness over 6 months. Based on results from a 20-month, multicenter, phase 3 RCT with 528 patients with POAG or ocular hypertension, both the 10 and 15 µg bimatoprost implant were noninferior to timolol in IOP lowering through 12 weeks. IOP lowering was similar after the second and third implant administrations and, interestingly, no additional treatment was needed for IOP lowering for an additional 12 months after the third administration of either implant. The most common treatment-associated adverse effect was conjunctival hyperemia that was typically temporary and associated with the administration procedure. Loss in mean corneal endothelial cell density was more frequent with the higher-dose implant and was ~ 5% in 10 µg implant-treated eyes and ~ 1% in topical timolol-treated eyes from baseline at 20 months. Visual field progression was reduced in the 10 µg implant group compared with the timolol group.
Beta-blockers as monotherapy and adjunctive to PGAs

A single RCT of adults with low-pressure glaucoma found less visual field progression at 4 years for participants randomized to brimonidine (5/45),a selective alpha-adrenergic agonist, vs. timolol (18/56), a beta-blocker, but attrition was high (40.5%) and unbalanced between groups and outcomes such as visual acuity or vertical cup-disc ratio were not reported. Ocular allergy was the most common side effect and occurred more often in the brimonidine group.

Brimonidine was not as effective in reducing IOP as timolol for adjunctive therapy to PGAs in an RCT of 152 patients with normal-tension glaucoma treated with PGA for at least 90 days who required additional treatment; discontinuation rates were similar and low (2.8% and 2.7%, respectively).

listitem.strong: Rho kinase inhibitors (Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase [ROCK])

list.listitem: Rho kinase inhibitors act by increasing outflow of aqueous humor through the conventional trabecular pathway by relaxing trabecular meshwork tissue. Ripasudil was first approved in Japan in 2014 and netarsudil (also a norepinephrine transporter inhibitor) and combination latanoprost/netarsudil in the U.S. in 2019.

Ripasudil hydrochloride hydrate, taken twice daily had an additive IOP-lowering effect of 0.9 to 1.6 mm Hg compared to placebo in combination with timolol and at peak level in combination with latanoprost in two RCTs.

In two RCTs with 1167 patients, once-daily dosing of netarsudil 0.02% was found to effective, with significant reductions in IOP from baseline, and noninferior to timolol. In a third RCT with 186 patients with POAG or ocular hypertension, once daily netarsudil 0.02% ophthalmic solution was noninferior to twice daily timolol 0.5% ophthalmic solution with mean reductions in IOP from baseline of 3.9 to 4.7 mmHg and 3.8 to 5.2 mmHg, respectively. Treatment effect was sustained over 6 months and conjunctival hyperemia, primarily mild, occurred in 47.9% of patients on netarsudil.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies found effective IOP reduction noninferior for rho kinase inhibitors compared to timolol as monotherapy and as adjunctive therapy, with a treatment duration of 1-3 months.

Omidenepag isopropyl 0.002%, a selective, non-prostaglandin, prostanoid EP2 receptor agonist, was noninferior to latanoprost 0.005% (once daily for 4 weeks) for reduction of IOP in a Japanese RCT of 190 patients with POAG or ocular hypertension.

Adverse effects of medications include: (1) topical PGAs: may cause hyperpigmentation of iris and periorbital skin, conjunctival hyperemia; (2) topical beta adrenergic antagonist: contraindicated in patients with heart block and asthma, may cause fatigue, depression, insomnia; (3) alpha adrenergic agonist: may cause redness, irritation, burning; (4) topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: contains sulfa compound and may cause redness, irritation; (5) oral/parenteral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: may cause paresthesia of fingers and toes, increased nephrolithiasis,aplastic anemia; (6) topical parasympathomimetics: may cause brow ache, blurred vision; and (7) oral hyperosmotics: may cause nausea vomiting, hyperglycemia; (8) topical rho kinase inhibitors: conjunctival hyperemia, usually transient and mild, and less commonly blepharitis, conjunctival hemorrhage, and allergic conjunctivitis.

Perioperative medication: Authors of a Cochrane review of 22 small RCTs found that perioperative antiglaucoma medications were superior to no medication or placebo for preventing IOP spikes >10 mmHg during the first two hours and up to 24 hours after laser trabeculoplasty for OAG.

In a study of intraoperative sub-Tenon injection of triamcinolone acetonide as an adjunct to Ahmed glaucoma valve implantation, patients randomized to the steroid injection had lower IOP at 1 month but there were no differences in groups at 12 months; peak postoperative IOP was significantly lower in the TA group (19.3 ± 4.8 mm Hg vs. 29 ± 9.2 mm Hg).

Similarly, in an RCT with 62 patients undergoing Ahmed glaucoma valve implantation, preoperative betamethasone eye drops vs. placebo resulted in significantly more patients with an IOP <18 mmHg at 6 months and a reduction in the number of anti-glaucoma medications used postoperatively at 1 year follow-up.

Based on a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs on selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) with 235 eyes receiving anti-inflammatory treatment and 170 eyes receiving placebo agents, there was no significant benefit on IOP reduction for between those receiving treatment vs. placebo; there were also no differences in clinical discomfort or anterior chamber inflammation 1 hour to 1-week post-procedure.

However, in one RCT with 85 patients undergoing SLT randomized to ketorolac 0.5%, prednisolone 1%, or saline tears distributed as unmarked drops to be used 4 times daily for 5 days, there were no statistically significant differences in IOP between groups at 6 week, but at 12 weeks both the NSAID and steroid groups had a statistically significantly greater decreases in IOP compared with placebo (mean, -6.2±3.1 mmHg, -5.2±2.7 mmHg, and -3±4.3 mmHg, respectively).

Use of intraoperative 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) and regular-dose postoperative 5-FU as an adjunct to trabeculectomy reduces surgical failure and IOP at one year in those undergoing primary trabeculectomy and for eyes at high risk of failure. 5-FU is used to inhibit wound healing to prevent conjunctival scarring. The 5-FU group, however, had a higher risk of complications and 5-FU is not currently being used routinely.

For PACG, obtain ophthalmology consult for evaluation and to start a topical beta-blocker, topical alpha-adrenergic agonist, topical miotic, oral/parenteral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, and/or oral or parenteral hyperosmotic agents if needed. Control pain and vomiting. Recheck IOP in 1 hour and repeat medications; consider adding IV mannitol if no improvement. If no IOP improvement after 2 hours, laser peripheral iridotomy should be considered.

In an RCT of 42 patients with PACG, subconjunctival injection of 2.5 mg dexamethasone in addition to standard treatment resulted in lower IOP at 24 hours with less pain and higher rates of treatment success (79.7% vs. 54.9% in the control group). There were no differences in anterior chamber cells, anterior chamber flare or photophobia between groups.

In the early stages of PACG, laser iridotomy can be performed to create a hole in the peripheral iris and provide an alternative pathway for aqueous to flow from the posterior into the anterior chamber, bypassing the pupil. If the angle remains closed, argon laser peripheral iridoplasty is indicated. If IOP remains uncontrolled, other options include laser trabeculoplasty or filtration surgery.
Laser peripheral iridotomy for acute or chronic angle closure is as effective as surgical iridectomy to increase aqueous humor access to outflow pathway.

Residual angle closure after laser peripheral iridotomy is common. In a 1-year follow-up study of 181 Chinese patients with PACG treated with peripheral iridotomy, most (81.8%) had residual angle closure. This rate is much higher than reported in an earlier case series in which residual angle closure was seen in 27 (38.6%) of 70 eyes.

Laser iridoplasty: When laser iridotomy fails to open the anterior chamber angle, laser iridoplasty may be considered. This treatment works by pulling the peripheral iris tissue away from the TM. Authors of a Cochrane review identified only a single randomized trial with 158 patients comparing adjunctive laser peripheral iridoplasty to iridotomy alone for elevated IOP; no differences were found in using iridoplasty as an adjunct to iridotomy with respect to number of medications or need for surgery.

Among 63 patients with PACG, those randomized to mitomycin C-augmented phacotrabeculectomy had comparable outcomes with respect to IOP lowering and treatment success compared to phacoemulsification alone (58% vs. 62%, respectively for having IOP of 6 to 21 mm Hg, on no medications, and no signs of glaucoma progression). Phacotrabeculectomy was associated with more postoperative interventions.

In a retrospective analysis of long-term follow-up of patients with PACG enrolled in two RCTs comparing phacotrabeculectomy to phacoemulsification alone, the former was more effective at lowering IOP and had a lower mean number of glaucoma medications required (0.7 vs. 1.6, respectively) but was associated with more postoperative complications, up to 5 years after surgery (25 vs. 6, respectively).

Authors of a systematic review of the effect of cataract surgery on IOP found decreased IOP of -6.4 mmHg; 95% CI, -9.4 to -3.4 among patients with angle-closure glaucoma and -2.7 mmHg; 95% CI, 3.7 to -1.7 from baseline for those with open-angle glaucoma at follow-up of 12 months or longer.

Phacoemulsification (Phaco) is a cataract surgery in which the lens is emulsified with an ultrasonic handpiece and aspirated from the eye. Goniosynechialysis (GSL) is a surgical technique performed to strip the peripheral anterior synechiae from the trabecular surface in the angle. Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies of patients with PACG found IOP decreased significantly more after Phaco-GSL than Phaco alone but there were no other differences with respect to medication use or complication occurrence. Outcomes were comparable for Phaco-GSL and Phaco-trabeculectomy or Phaco-trabeculectomy for all measured outcomes.

listitem.strong: Patients with Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG) and those with refractory glaucoma

list.listitem: Although minimally invasive surgeries have good safety profiles and appear effective in lowering IOP and reducing use of glaucoma medications for individuals with POAG, there are few comparative studies and authors of this systematic review and meta-analysis found a number of concerns and risks of bias in current studies.
Laser trabeculoplasty to increase aqueous outflow is an effective adjunct to medical therapy, or is an option for patients who cannot tolerate topical or oral medications.

In an RCT of 718 patients with POAG or ocular hypertension only, there were no differences in health-related quality of life at 3 years between patients randomized to laser trabeculoplasty as initial treatment vs. eye drops. Slightly more patients were at target IOP with trabeculotomy (93% vs. 91.3% with eye drops). One quarter of the patients in the trabeculotomy group required medications to maintain IOP at target, however, laser trabeculotomy was determined to be more cost-effective.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 22 studies involving 2704 patients concluded that post-procedural IOP was not significantly different between types of laser trabeculoplasty; however, those undergoing 180-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty required fewer medications than those treated with argon laser trabeculoplasty at 12 months (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.06-0.50). No severe adverse outcomes were reported for any of the procedures.

Filtering surgery, with or without a tube-shunt implant, to create an alternate outflow for aqueous humor is an alternative to laser trabeculoplasty. In this surgery, a partial thickness flap is made in the sclera and a window opening is created under the flap to remove a portion of the sclera, Schlemm's canal, and the trabecular meshwork (trabeculectomy). Drainage of aqueous humor occurs through several mechanisms including around the flap margins into a filtering bleb that forms underneath the conjunctiva.
In an RCT of 120 patients, EX-PRESS implant filtration device was as effective as trabeculectomy with respect to mean IOPs, medication use, and surgical success at 2 years.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 RCTs with 808 patients found EX-PRESS compared with trabeculectomy resulted in a significant difference in IOP at 1 year; complete success of trabeculectomy was significantly lower than that of Ex-PRESS (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57-0.93).

listitem.strong: Aqueous shunts (connects two previously unconnected body parts) and stents (keeps blocked passageway open)

list.listitem: Authors of a review of 6 Cochrane reviews of minimally-invasive surgeries for POAG concluded that, compared with cataract surgery alone, adding a Hydrus stent improved the likelihood of drop-free glaucoma control at medium and long-term (RR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4 to 1.9) follow-up and conferred 2.0-mm Hg (95% CI -2.7 to -1.3 mm Hg) greater IOP reduction at long-term follow-up. iStent also safely improved drop-free disease control compared with cataract surgery alone (RR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2 to 1.6), but IOP-lowering was not sustained in the long term.

Aqueous shunts are used for patients who fail or are not candidates for surgery. Authors of a Cochrane review found sufficient to determine differences between aqueous shunts and trabeculectomy for glaucoma treatment. The Baerveldt implant appeared to lower IOP more than the Ahmed implant, but clinical significance was unclear. There are no data to confirm superiority of one surgical procedure or device over another.

At 5-year follow-up of 2 RCTs with 514 patients, those in the Baerveldt group compared to the Ahmed group had a lower failure rate (37% vs. 49%), lower rate of de novo glaucoma surgery (8% vs. 16%), and lower mean IOP on fewer medications; those receiving the Baerveldt implantation, however, had a higher risk of hypotony (4.5% vs. 0.4%).

In a report of 3-year results of 242 patients with medically-uncontrolled glaucoma and no previous incisional ocular surgery enrolled in the Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (with mitomycin C) Study, there were no significant differences between groups in surgical failure rate (33% in the tube group and 28% in the trabeculectomy group) or serious complications producing vision loss or requiring reoperation (3 patients (2%) in the tube group and 9 patients (8%) in the trabeculectomy group). More patients in the trabeculectomy group had lower IOP with fewer used glaucoma medications.
In an RCT comparing Ab-Externo Microshunt with trabeculectomy, both performed with adjunctive mitomycin C, the probability of success was lower with MicroShunt (53.9% vs. 72.7%, respectively).

Use of a supraciliary micro-stent for patients with POAG refractory to topical medications sufficiently lowered IOP in more than 80% of patients at 1 year in one case series. The most common adverse events were IOP increases >30 mm Hg beyond 1 month (11%, 7/65), transient hyphema (6%, 4/65), and cataract progression (12%, 5/41 phakic eyes).

In a 5-year follow-up of patients from the multicenter Study of an Implantable Device for Lowering Intraocular Pressure in Glaucoma Patients Undergoing Cataract Surgery trial who underwent either Micro-Stent implantation plus phacoemulsification (n = 215) or phacoemulsification alone (n = 67), more patients in the Micro-Stent group achieved a reduction of ≥20% in IOP without using hypotensive medication (46% vs. 32.1%, respectively). Only 3 sight-threatening serious ocular adverse events occurred 2 in the stent group that were unrelated to the stent

In a follow-up of 212 patients with medically-uncontrolled glaucoma who had previous cataract and/or glaucoma surgery, the 5-year cumulative reoperation rate was significantly higher among patients randomized to trabeculectomy with mitomycin C compared to those managed with a tube shunt (29% vs. 9%). Similar surgical outcomes with respect to IOP and number of medications were observed for these group.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 78 studies found XEN gel stent effective in lowering IOP and the number of anti-glaucoma medications. Although no significant difference was found between XEN and phaco-XEN surgery for IOP after surgery, number of anti-glaucoma medications and bleb needling rate were higher using XEN compared to phaco-XEN and bleb needling rate was higher than in trabeculectomy.
In a follow-up study of patients undergoing either a tube shunt or trabeculectomy with mitomycin C, quality-of-life outcomes were similar.

In an RCT comparing two shunts used for of 152 patients with elevated IOP, at 12 months, the Hydrus Microstent perfomed better than the iStent Trabecular Micro Bypass device in surgical success and being medication free for elevated IOP (22.6% difference); two patients in the iStent group required secondary glaucoma surgery. The Hydrus Microstent with cataract surgery in patients with POAG appears to increase the proportion of patients who do not require IOP lowering medication compared to cataract surgery alone, based on a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs. Larger studies are needed to assess complication rates.

In an RCT comparing primary medical management with primary surgical treatment (augmented trabeculectomy) in patients with primary open-angle glaucoma presenting with advanced disease, there were no differences in visual function/health-related quality of life between treatment arms at 24 months. Mean IOP was significantly lower in the surgical treatment arm (12.40 mmHg vs. 15.07 mmHg, respectively).

Trabeculectomy is more effective than non-penetrating surgeries for reducing IOP in patients with POAG based on a systematic review of 18 trials (mean between-group difference −2.15 mm Hg; 95% CI, −2.85 to −1.44). However, there is a higher risk of complications such as cataract and flat or shallow anterior chamber following trabeculectomy. Investigators in one RCT found no difference in need for repeat surgery or uncontrolled IOP between fornix- vs limbal-based trabeculectomy, but increased risk of shallow anterior chamber in the limbal-based group.

Intraoperative trabeculectomy with beta-radiation (to slow healing) vs. trabeculectomy alone appears to lower the risk of surgical failure (pooled risk ratio (RR) 0.23; 95% CI, 0.14-0.40) but increases the risk of cataract (RR 2.89; 95% CI, 1.39-6.0).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs found bevacizumab as adjunct to trabeculectomy more effective than placebo with respect to complete success rate, decreased IOP at 6 months after trabeculectomy and number of antiglaucoma medications. However, compared with mitomycin C, bevacizumab significantly increased the rate of encysted blebs.
In a recent RCT, the two drugs were comparable with respect to reducing IOP at 1 year following trabeculectomy, and bevacizumab had significantly higher rates exhibiting low bleb vascularity.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 small studies comparing trabeculectomy with either mitomycin-C or implant found higher IOP-lowering efficacy with the former but also a higher risk of post-surgery hypotony and suture lysis. There were no differences in treatment success or incidence of other complications between groups.
This procedure reduces the rate of aqueous production and is usually reserved for eyes with decreased vision.

In a meta-analysis of 6 small RCTs comparing cyclophotocoagulation and alternative surgical techniques in the treatment of refractory glaucoma, authors found no differences in lowered postoperative IOP between groups. Data on safety and complications will require further study.

Among patients with neovascular glaucoma, authors of a meta-analysis concluded that interferon and mitomycin plus trabeculectomy (94.9%), glaucoma valve implantation (86.9%), and iris photocoagulation plus trabeculectomy (81.9%) were the most likely to improve treatment success. In another meta-analysis of 23 studies with 1303 patients treated with 6 different interventions for neovascular glaucoma, the most effective treatments for reducing IOP at 6 months were Ahmed glaucoma valve implant surgery combined with intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor and cyclophotocoagulation compared with Ahmed glaucoma valve implant alone, cyclocryotherapy, trabeculectomy with mitomycin and trabeculectomy combined with intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor.

In a Japanese RCT comparing Baerveldt glaucoma implantation with trabeculectomy for 50 patients with neovascular glaucoma, there were similar success rates (59.1% and 61.6% at 1-year, respectively) and no statistical differences in postoperative IOP measured at 6-month intervals.

Authors of a guideline on Chinese herbal medicine for POAG conducted a meta-analysis of 36 RCTs, described syndromes associated with elevated IOP, and concluded that supporting evidence was strongest for use of erigeron breviscapus tablets for blood stasis and fluid retention syndrome. The authors also provided expert consensus opinion for other herbal medicines for these syndromes.
Cochrane authors were unable to determine whether acupuncture is helpful for glaucoma based on 3 RCTs and an ongoing trial, all at high risk of bias and with large quantities of missing data.

In a 2015 small RCT/crossover study with a 50% drop-out rate, acupuncture had no effect on diurnal IOP or best-corrected visual acuity. IOP increased temporarily immediately after the acupuncture session.

Visual field loss associated with glaucoma may be partly reversible. Behavioral vision training vs. placebo training led to greater improvements in detection accuracy in high-resolution perimetry and faster reaction time in a small RCT of 30 patients with glaucoma who had stable visual fields and well-controlled IOP. There were no differences in quality-of-life measures which improved in both groups. The training focused on activation of areas of residual vision using computer-based daily 1-hour vision training sessions over 3 months.
Optimizing home lighting may also be of benefit.

Medication adherence is important in reducing progression of glaucoma and visual field loss. In a long-term follow-up study of 307 patients randomized to the medication arm of a trial, after an average of 7.3 years, the 142 (46%) subjects who reported never missing a medication dose had an average predicted mean deviation loss of 0.62 dB, consistent with age-related loss while those reporting missing medication doses at one third of visits had a loss of 1.42 dB and subjects who reported missing medication doses at two thirds of visits had a loss of 2.23 dB.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 7 studies of patient education to promote adherence to eye drops for glaucoma found that interventions combining patient education with personalized behavior-change interventions (e.g., tailoring daily routines to promote adherence) may improve adherence; data were insufficient to recommend a particular intervention. In another systematic review, 5 of 8 studies found improved adherence through educational intervention.
Reminder calls, but not motivational interviewing, led to better medication adherence than usual care in one study.

In a cohort of 127 subjects enrolled in the Low-Pressure Glaucoma Treatment Study, risk factors for optic disc hemorrhage included migraine headache, low systolic blood pressure and mean arterial ocular perfusion pressure, and use of systemic beta-blockers.

Among 1618 participants in the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study, the incidence of optic disc hemorrhage was 0.5% per year during an average of 13 years before development of POAG and 1.2% per year during an average of 6 years after the development of POAG. The occurrence of a disc hemorrhage increased the risk of developing POAG 2.6-fold; 95% CI, 1.7-4.0.

The reintervention rate following glaucoma filtering surgery was 1.84 (95% CI 1.57-2.13). There was a lower rate for Baerveldt implant (0.53, 95% CI 0.29-0.83) and Preserflo Ab-Externo Microshunt (0.60, 95% CI 0.15-1.29), and a higher rate for Xen gel shunt (4.26, 95% CI 2.59-6.31).

In a follow-up study of 334 patients with 460 eyes that underwent trabeculectomy, 45% experienced a complication within the 20-year follow-up. Vision-threatening complications were much less frequent with cumulative probabilities during the 20 years of 2.0% (95% CI, 0%-4.0%) for blebitis and 5.0% (95% CI, 1.0%-9.0%) for endophthalmitis.

Encapsulation of the trabecular bleb is an early post-operative cause of treatment failure. While observational studies reported success with needling this bleb to re-establish drainage vs. restarting medication, no difference in reducing IOP was found between these treatments in the single small RCT of 25 eyes.

The reported natural course of untreated subjects without glaucomatous disc cupping or visual field loss in the face of elevated IOP, so called ocular hypertension, is the development of early glaucomatous visual field loss emerging at a rate of approximately 1% per year. B
Topical ocular hypotensive medications are effective in delaying or preventing the onset of POAG in individuals with elevated IOP. A

Risk factors for progression include higher baseline and mean IOP, older age, disc hemorrhage, large cup-to-disc ration or small optic nerve rim area, beta-zone parapapillary atrophy, thinner central cornea with GAT IOP measurement, decreased corneal hysteresis, lower ocular perfusion pressure, pseudoexfoliation, and poor medication adherence.

In a meta-analysis of 23 population-based studies with 78,434 participants, POAG was diagnosed in 1702 persons including 151 (8.9%) who were blind. PACG was more likely to be associated with blindness; there were 724 cases of PACG with 196 (27.0%) who were blind. The cumulative risk ratio of blindness in PACG vs. POAG was 2.39 (95% CI 1.99, 2.87)

Follow-up should include IOP checks between every 3 and 6 months, gonioscopy at initial exam and repeated as necessary, optic nerve exam 1 to 3 times a year, and visual field testing 1 to 3 times a year. Follow-up intervals of 1-2 months are recommended by AAO consensus if there is evidence of progressive damage.
Gonioscopy is performed following treatment for PACG to verify improvement in angle configuration or if there is unexplained change in IOP.

Among patients enrolled in the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial and followed with field testing and optic disc photographs, glaucoma progression was detected first in the visual field in 80%, 79% and 100% in patients with early visual field loss, moderate field loss, and advanced field loss, respectively.

For patients with advanced glaucoma, the AAO suggests adjusting computerized visual field programs (24 degrees, 30 degrees, 10 degrees) and varying stimulus size for monitoring progressive visual field loss.
Ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer thickness measured by spectral-domain optical coherence tomography may be the best measure for detecting progression.

In one study, combining visual field testing with optical coherence tomography evidence of optic nerve damage using the structure-guided ANSWERS method appeared to be the most effective method for detecting glaucoma progression than the reference and other visual field-only methods.

Data on risks of use of topical ocular hypotensive agents during pregnancy are limited. Most agents are described as having evidence of adverse fetal effects in animal reproductive studies, without well-controlled studies on pregnant women (formerly pregnancy category C) with the exception of brimonidine which has not been observed to cause teratogenic effects in animal studies (previously pregnancy category B). Brimonidine, however, is known to cross the blood-brain barrier. Although it is not known if it is excreted in breastmilk, it should be avoided in breastfeeding due to hypothetical risk of apnea in infants unless there is a compelling indication for use. There is a theoretical risk of premature labor with use of prostaglandins, and if they must be used, should be used with punctal occlusion. The AAO notes that these medications may be considered for use during breastfeeding. Ophthalmic prostaglandins should be administered after breastfeeding to reduce the potential expsoure to the infant.
According to the AAO, the definition of childhood glaucoma is IOP-related damage to the eye, a diagnosis met only after multiple evaluations establishing progressive change.

Childhood glaucoma is rare, with an incidence of 2.29 per 100,000 for patients <20 years of age. In the Olmstead County population study, 5/30 cases were primary congenital, 6/30 were secondary to other conditions (e.g., Sturge-Weber Syndrome) and 19/30 were acquired (e.g., trauma). A family history of glaucoma was present in 20% of the children, the mean IOP at baseline was 30.8 mm Hg (range, 14-56 mm Hg), and half had bilateral disease.

Following surgery with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation for infantile cataracts, eighty patients (17.0%) in one cohort developed glaucoma at a median follow-up of 4.3 years. Risk factors for risk for postoperative glaucoma in multivariable analysis were primary implantation (lower; HR 0.10; 95% CI, 0.01-0.76) and additional intraocular surgery (HR 2.25; 95% CI, 1.20-4.21). However, in a RCT of children with unilateral congenital cataract, rates of glaucoma at 4.8 years after surgery were not significantly different between primary IOL and no IOL implantation. Rather, younger age was significantly associated with glaucoma (HR 3.2; 95% CI, 1.2-8.3), which occurred in 17% of patients (glaucoma + suspected glaucoma occurred in 31%).

There are no specific recommendations for screening for glaucoma in children. The American Academy of Family Physicians and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (2017) recommend vision screening (visual acuity and alignment) at least once in all children between the ages of 3 and 5 years to detect amblyopia or its risk factors. B For younger children, there is insufficient evidence for assessing the balance of benefits and harms of vision screening. Newborn screening generally consists of red reflex (can be abnormal in cases of glaucoma), external inspection and pupillary examination.
Symptoms of glaucoma in children include photophobia, tears overflowing onto the face (epiphora), and involuntary tight eyelid closure (blepharospasm).

In a retrospective study of 108 children diagnosed with glaucoma over a 10-year period, 64% were males and mean age at diagnosis was 7.07±5.4 years. Almost all (92%) had refractive errors and 85% of them had astigmatism. “Glaucoma suspect” was the most prevalent category (46%), followed by glaucoma associated with acquired ocular anomaly (20%), juvenile open-angle glaucoma (16%) and primary congenital glaucoma (3%, all males).

The diagnosis of glaucoma in children requires two or more of the following (AAO, 2015): IOP >21 mm Hg not under anesthesia Optic disc cupping: progressive increase in cup-disc ratio, cup-disc asymmetry of ≥0.2 when the optic discs are similar size, or focal rim thinning Corneal findings of Haab striae or diameter ≥11 mm in newborn, >12 mm in child <1 year, or >13 mm any age Progressive myopia, myopic shift, or an increase in ocular dimensions out of keeping with normal growth Reproducible visual-field defect consistent with glaucomatous optic neuropathy with no other observable reason for defect
Childhood glaucoma can be treated medically or surgically, with most cases of primary glaucoma treated surgically with trabeculotomy.

In children with primary congenital glaucoma, illuminated microcatheter-assisted circumferential trabeculotomy achieved comparable surgical outcomes to mitomycin C-augmented combined trabeculotomy-trabeculectomy with absolute success at one year of 86.7% (26/30) and 90.0% (27/30), respectively. The incidence of hyphema was significantly more in infants randomized to the microcatheter group.

In a small RCT of 40 eyes in 31 children with primary congenital glaucoma, absolute success rates were higher in those randomized to microcatheter-assisted circumferential trabeculotomy compared to conventional partial trabeculotomy (80% [16/20] and 60% [12/20], respectively).

Similarly, in a RCT of 62 children with congenital glaucoma, those randomized to Glaucolight illuminated microcatheter trabeculotomy had higher success rates at 2 years compared to those receiving a rigid-probe trabeculotomy (67% vs. 47%, respectively).

In an RCT of trabeculectomy in 20 children with OAG in which one eye was treated with ologen and the other with mitomycin C, at 1 year, ologen was more successful in reducing IOP and resulted in fewer complications.

In a follow-up of children with congenital glaucoma, successful treatment with angle surgery at 10 years occurred in 83 of 110 eyes (75.5%). Although age at presentation did not affect surgical success, children diagnosed at <3 months of age had a visual outcome <20/200 despite successful glaucoma control.

For children with continued elevation of IOP after glaucoma surgery, investigators in a case series of 35 children and 57 eyes found 84.3% responded to medical treatment with latanoprost alone or in combination with dorzolamide at 1 year follow up with only mild local adverse effects reported and no medication withdrawals due to adverse events.
